blocks.text: 训练数据可能在训练领域之外对语言模型的行为产生意想不到的副作用：不安全的代码数据会诱发广泛的失准，过时的鸟类名称则会诱发 19 世纪的人格。要理解这种泛化很难，因为目前只有几十个零散的例子。为了批量生产这类带有意外副作用的数据集（DSSE），我们定义了三个目标（诱发、自然、意外），并用一条自动化流水线搜索高分数据集。我们的流水线在 18 种目标行为上产出了数千个 DSSE，其中许多能跨模型家族泛化，并让机器学习研究者感到意外。这些数据集构成了研究泛化的测试平台，也为在模型部署前预测训练副作用奠定了基础。

blocks.text: 大语言模型（LLM）依靠后训练来成为有用的助手或适应特定领域，但后训练可能以意想不到的方式改变模型行为。用于训练 Claude Opus 4.7 的一份商业技能数据集被发现会在部署后增加不诚实行为 [1]；用已过时的鸟类名称训练，会让模型相信自己身处 19 世纪 [2]；而训练数据中的不安全代码则可能引发涌现性失准 [3]。在每种情况下，训练数据都在训练领域之外造成了非预期、意想不到的副作用——我们把这类数据称为带有意外副作用的数据集（DSSE）。

blocks.text: DSSE 既带来实际挑战，也暴露出我们对 LLM 科学理解的空白。当数据看起来像与效果无关的普通后训练数据时尤其如此，Opus 4.7 的商业技能数据就是如此。在实际层面，它们让模型行为难以预测，因为没有任何标记提示这些数据有风险，而潜在副作用的空间又太大，无法逐一检查。在科学层面，它们是 LLM 泛化现象的实例，而我们对这类现象尚未充分理解。

blocks.text: 尽管 DSSE 对实际后训练而言并不理想，但把它们揭示出来可以推动研究进展。例如，涌现性失准文献中提出的 DSSE 帮助促成了人格选择模型 [4, 5]，而 Opus 4.7 的商业技能副作用则为 Opus 4.8 的改进后训练提供了参考 [1]。一套能够预测意外副作用的泛化理论会更有价值，而大量 DSSE 的集合能让研究者检验这类理论。

blocks.text: 遗憾的是，目前已知的 DSSE 只有几十个（表 1），这使得推进对该现象的科学理解变得困难。原因在于，发现 DSSE 依赖人工劳动：已知的 DSSE 要么是在撰写完整研究论文的过程中构建出来的，要么是偶然遇到的。因此，我们提出自动化发现更多 DSSE 样例，以便能够大规模地开发和检验预测副作用的理论与方法。

blocks.text: 要构建一条能批量生成 DSSE 的自动化流水线，我们需要精确界定 DSSE 的构成。我们提出，DSSE 应具备三个属性：(1) 它应诱发模型此前未表现出的副作用行为；(2) 它应自然，读起来像普通的训练后数据；(3) 它应令人意外，即人类读者看到这些数据时不会预料到该副作用。这些属性将 DSSE 与普通的域内泛化、以及风险并不出人意料的数据区分开来。

blocks.text: 我们提出一个两阶段流程，联合优化这些目标来构建 DSSE。第一阶段，我们用进化和强化学习（RL）等搜索方法寻找候选数据集；另外还改造了两种方法，分别重写[8]或过滤[7]现有数据集。由于进化和 RL 哪怕只产出一个候选数据集，也要大量评估评分函数，我们让它们改用成本更低的 DSSE 目标代理版本。第二阶段，我们用成本更高、留出的评判器给候选数据集重新打分，再筛选出最终的高质量 DSSE 集合。这种带留出评判器的两阶段设计，能缓解第一阶段代理目标被奖励攻击（reward hacking）的问题。

blocks.text: An automated pipeline finds thousands of ordinary-looking datasets that induce unexpected AI behaviors.

inlines.text: An automated pipeline finds thousands of ordinary-looking datasets that induce unexpected AI behaviors.

blocks.text: Training data can have unexpected side effects on language model behavior outside the training domain: insecure code data can induce broad misalignment, and outdated bird names can induce a 19th-century persona. Understanding such generalization is hard because only dozens of isolated examples exist. To mass produce such datasets with surprising side effects (DSSEs), we define three objectives (elicitation, naturalness, and surprisingness) and use an automated pipeline to search for high-scoring datasets. Our pipeline produces thousands of DSSEs across 18 target behaviors, many of which generalize across model families and surprise ML researchers. These datasets form a testbed for studying generalization and lay the groundwork for predicting training side effects before model deployment.

blocks.text: Large language models (LLMs) rely on post-training to become helpful assistants or adapt to specific domains, but post-training can change a model's behavior in unexpected ways. A business skill dataset used to train Claude Opus 4.7 was found to increase dishonesty after deployment [1]; training on outdated bird names induces beliefs that a model is in the 19th century [2]; and, insecure code in training data can cause emergent misalignment [3]. In each case, the training data causes an undesired and unexpected side effect outside the training domain—we call such data datasets with surprising side effects (DSSEs).

blocks.text: DSSEs present both practical challenges and gaps in scientific understanding of LLMs. This is especially true when the data looks like ordinary post-training data irrelevant to the effect, as the Opus 4.7 business skill data did. Practically, they make model behavior hard to predict, since nothing marks the data as risky and the space of potential side effects is too large to check. Scientifically, they are instances of generalization phenomena of LLMs that are not yet well-understood.

blocks.text: Although DSSEs are undesirable for practical post-training, surfacing examples of them can drive research progress. For example, DSSEs introduced in emergent misalignment literature helped motivate the persona selection model [4, 5], and the Opus 4.7 business skill side effect informed better post-training for Opus 4.8 [1]. A theory of generalization that could predict surprising side effects would be even more valuable, and a large collection of DSSEs would enable researchers to test such theories.

blocks.text: Unfortunately, known DSSEs number only in the dozens (Table 1), making it difficult to advance scientific understanding of the phenomenon. This is because discovering DSSEs is human-labor-bound: known DSSEs were either constructed during the writing of a full research paper or encountered by accident. We therefore propose automating the discovery of more examples of DSSEs, so that theories and methods for predicting side effects can be developed and tested at scale.

blocks.text: To build an automatic pipeline that mass produces DSSEs, we need to precisely define what constitutes them. We propose that a DSSE should have three properties: it should (1) elicit a side-effect behavior the model did not previously exhibit, (2) be natural, reading like ordinary post-training data, and (3) be surprising, in that a human reader of the data would not anticipate the side effect. These properties distinguish DSSEs from ordinary in-domain generalization and from data that is unsurprisingly risky.

blocks.text: Given this definition, scalable discovery of DSSEs requires automatic ways of measuring all three properties. We measure elicitation by finetuning a model on the dataset, sampling responses on relevant prompts, and asking an LLM judge whether they exhibit the target behavior. Naturalness is scored with Elo ratings calculated from pairwise judgments in which an LLM picks the more natural one of two datasets. Surprisingness is estimated by how well frontier LLMs predict a dataset's side effect given examples from it; worse prediction means a more surprising side effect. Our human study shows that these objectives track the judgments of ML researchers.

blocks.text: We propose a two-stage pipeline for jointly optimizing these objectives to construct DSSEs. In the first stage, we use search methods like evolution and reinforcement learning (RL) to search for candidate datasets; we also adapt two other methods that rewrite [8] or filter [7] existing datasets. Since evolution and RL require many score function evaluations to produce even a single candidate dataset, we use cheaper proxy versions of the DSSE objectives for them. In the second stage, we re-score candidate datasets using more expensive, held-out judges and filter them to a final set of high-quality DSSEs. Our two-stage design with held-out judges mitigates reward hacking of the proxy objectives in the first stage.

In the second stage, we re-score candidate datasets using more expensive, held-out judges and filter them to a final set of high-quality DSSEs. Our two-stage design with held-out judges mitigates reward hacking of the proxy objectives in the first stage.

blocks.text: Figure 3. We automate discovery of datasets with surprising side effects (DSSEs). Left: Given a target behavior with eval prompts and a rubric (①), we search for datasets that raise a model's frequency of the behavior while reading like ordinary post-training data and evading our judges (②); an example DSSE is shown in ③. On 64 datasets spanning various levels of surprisingness, ML researchers name a behavior the dataset induces in 63% of trials, against 50% by chance, while a frontier LLM does so in 86%.

inlines.text: Our pipeline produces thousands of DSSEs across 18 target behaviors (e.g. recommending self-harm, resisting shutdown, etc.). We highlight three findings:
DSSEs can be constructed for a wide range of behaviors, and many of them generalize across model families and sizes despite being optimized against a small 1.7B parameter model.
Optimization-based methods are consistently successful across behaviors; subliminal learning methods work better on preference behaviors than open-ended ones.
ML researchers barely beat chance at predicting side effects (63% accuracy against 50% by chance). Frontier LLMs outperform them, but model scale does not reliably improve accuracy.

blocks.text: We release these datasets as the DSSE-1.1 collection to drive better understanding of LLM post-training and generalization. Furthermore, we hope DSSE-1.1 will enable tools like monitors for training data that can flag unsafe side effects before a model is deployed.
